claim: Allopregnanolone (3α5αP) binds to the canonical β3(+)–α1(-) intersubunit site in α1β3 GABAA receptors.
source: We found that the potentiating neurosteroid, allopregnanolone, but not its inhibitory 3β-epimer epi-allopregnanolone, binds to the canonical β3(+)–α1(-) intersubunit site that mediates receptor activation by neurosteroids.
evidence: Supported by photolabeling competition experiments showing that 3α5αP prevents KK200 photolabeling of β3G308 in the intersubunit site (Figure 4C).

claim: Epi-allopregnanolone (3β5αP) does not bind to the canonical β3(+)–α1(-) intersubunit site in α1β3 GABAA receptors.
source: We found that the potentiating neurosteroid, allopregnanolone, but not its inhibitory 3β-epimer epi-allopregnanolone, binds to the canonical β3(+)–α1(-) intersubunit site that mediates receptor activation by neurosteroids.
evidence: Supported by photolabeling competition experiments showing that 3β5αP did not prevent KK200 photolabeling of β3G308 in the intersubunit site (Figure 4C).

claim: Both allopregnanolone and epi-allopregnanolone bind to intrasubunit sites in the β3 subunit.
source: In contrast, both allopregnanolone and epi-allopregnanolone bind to intrasubunit sites in the β3 subunit, promoting receptor desensitization and the α1 subunit promoting effects that vary between neurosteroids.
evidence: Supported by photolabeling competition experiments showing both steroids prevent KK123 photolabeling at β3 intrasubunit sites (Figure 5B).

claim: Both allopregnanolone and epi-allopregnanolone bind to intrasubunit sites in the α1 subunit.
source: In contrast, both allopregnanolone and epi-allopregnanolone bind to intrasubunit sites in the β3 subunit, promoting receptor desensitization and the α1 subunit promoting effects that vary between neurosteroids.
evidence: Supported by photolabeling competition experiments showing both steroids prevent KK200 and KK123 photolabeling at α1 intrasubunit sites (Figure 4B, Figure 5C).

claim: Binding of neurosteroids to β3 and α1 intrasubunit sites promotes receptor desensitization.
source: In contrast, both allopregnanolone and epi-allopregnanolone bind to intrasubunit sites in the β3 subunit, promoting receptor desensitization and the α1 subunit promoting effects that vary between neurosteroids.
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological data showing mutations in intrasubunit sites reduce desensitization by 3β5αP (Figure 9B).

claim: KK148 and KK150 bind to all three neurosteroid-binding sites on α1β3 GABAARs.
source: Two neurosteroid analogues with diazirine moieties replacing the 3-hydroxyl (KK148 and KK150) bind to all three sites, but do not potentiate GABAAR currents.
evidence: Supported by photolabeling competition experiments showing KK148 and KK150 prevent KK200 photolabeling at both intersubunit and intrasubunit sites (Figure 4B-C), and direct photolabeling showing adducts at α1 and β3 intrasubunit sites (Figure 4D-E, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).

claim: KK148 and KK150 do not potentiate GABAAR currents.
source: Two neurosteroid analogues with diazirine moieties replacing the 3-hydroxyl (KK148 and KK150) bind to all three sites, but do not potentiate GABAAR currents.
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological recordings showing no potentiation of GABA-elicited currents by KK148 or KK150 (Figure 1C-D).

claim: KK148 is a desensitizing agent.
source: KK148 is a desensitizing agent, whereas KK150 is devoid of allosteric activity.
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological data showing KK148 reduces steady-state currents (Figure 2A) and enhances [3H]muscimol binding (Figure 1E).

claim: KK150 is devoid of allosteric activity.
source: KK148 is a desensitizing agent, whereas KK150 is devoid of allosteric activity.
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological data showing KK150 does not reduce steady-state currents (Figure 2B) and minimally enhances [3H]muscimol binding (Figure 1E).

claim: Differential occupancy and efficacy at three discrete neurosteroid-binding sites determine whether a neurosteroid has potentiating, inhibitory, or competitive antagonist activity on GABAARs.
source: Collectively, these data show that differential occupancy and efficacy at three discrete neurosteroid-binding sites determine whether a neurosteroid has potentiating, inhibitory, or competitive antagonist activity on GABAARs.
evidence: Supported by the combined photolabeling, binding, and electrophysiological data showing different neurosteroids bind to different subsets of sites with different functional outcomes.

claim: Neurosteroids are endogenous modulators of brain development and function.
source: Neurosteroids (NS) are endogenous modulators of brain development and function and are important mediators of mood (Belelli and Lambert, 2005; Mitchell et al., 2008; Represa and Ben-Ari, 2005; Grobin et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Neurosteroids are important mediators of mood.
source: Neurosteroids (NS) are endogenous modulators of brain development and function and are important mediators of mood (Belelli and Lambert, 2005; Mitchell et al., 2008; Represa and Ben-Ari, 2005; Grobin et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Exogenously administered neurosteroid analogues have been clinically used as anesthetics and anti-depressants.
source: Exogenously administered NS analogues have been clinically used as anesthetics and anti-depressants and have therapeutic potential as anti-epileptics, neuroprotective agents and cognitive enhancers (Belelli and Lambert, 2005; Mitchell et al., 2008; Akk et al., 2007; Reddy and Estes, 2016; Kharasch and Hollmann, 2015; Gunduz-Bruce et al., 2019; Zorumski et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Neurosteroid analogues have therapeutic potential as anti-epileptics, neuroprotective agents and cognitive enhancers.
source: Exogenously administered NS analogues have been clinically used as anesthetics and anti-depressants and have therapeutic potential as anti-epileptics, neuroprotective agents and cognitive enhancers (Belelli and Lambert, 2005; Mitchell et al., 2008; Akk et al., 2007; Reddy and Estes, 2016; Kharasch and Hollmann, 2015; Gunduz-Bruce et al., 2019; Zorumski et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The principal target of neurosteroids is the γ-aminobutyric acid type A receptor (GABAAR).
source: The principal target of NS is the γ-aminobutyric acid type A receptor (GABAAR).
evidence: Supported by established scientific knowledge and citations throughout the manuscript.

claim: Neurosteroids can either activate or inhibit GABAARs.
source: NS can either activate or inhibit GABAARs.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature and data in the manuscript.

claim: Positive allosteric modulatory neurosteroids such as allopregnanolone potentiate the effect of GABA on GABAAR currents at low concentrations.
source: Positive allosteric modulatory NS (PAM-NS) such as allopregnanolone (3α5αP) potentiate the effect of GABA on GABAAR currents at low concentrations and directly activate the receptors at higher concentrations (Akk et al., 2007; Akk et al., 2010; Chen et al., 2019; Olsen, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature and data showing 3α5αP potentiation (Figure 1A).

claim: Positive allosteric modulatory neurosteroids directly activate GABAARs at higher concentrations.
source: Positive allosteric modulatory NS (PAM-NS) such as allopregnanolone (3α5αP) potentiate the effect of GABA on GABAAR currents at low concentrations and directly activate the receptors at higher concentrations (Akk et al., 2007; Akk et al., 2010; Chen et al., 2019; Olsen, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Negative allosteric modulatory neurosteroids such as epi-allopregnanolone or pregnenolone sulfate inhibit GABAAR currents.
source: Negative allosteric modulatory NS (NAM-NS), such as epi-allopregnanolone (3β5αP) or pregnenolone sulfate (PS) inhibit GABAAR currents (Akk et al., 2001; Wang et al., 2002; Shen et al., 2000; Lundgren et al., 2003; Seljeset et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature and data showing 3β5αP reduces steady-state currents (Figure 2C).

claim: PAM-NS increase the affinity of the GABAAR for orthosteric ligand binding.
source: In addition to enhancing channel opening, PAM-NS increase the affinity of the GABAAR for orthosteric ligand binding, an effect thought to be mechanistically linked to channel gating (Chen et al., 2019; Harrison et al., 1987a).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature and data showing 3α5αP enhances [3H]muscimol binding (Figure 1E).

claim: GABAARs are pentameric ligand-gated ion channels composed of two α-subunits, two β-subunits and one additional subunit.
source: GABAARs are pentameric ligand-gated ion channels (pLGIC) composed of two α-subunits (α1–6), two β-subunits (β1–3) and one additional subunit (γ1–3, δ, ε, θ or π) (Sigel and Steinmann, 2012; Sieghart, 2015; Olsen and Sieghart, 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature and established scientific knowledge.

claim: Each GABAAR subunit is composed of a large extracellular domain, a transmembrane domain formed by four membrane-spanning helices, a long intracellular loop between TM3 and TM4, and a short extracellular C-terminus.
source: Each subunit is composed of a large extracellular domain (ECD), a transmembrane domain (TMD) formed by four membrane-spanning helices (TM1-4), a long intracellular loop between TM3 and TM4, and a short extracellular C-terminus (Akk et al., 2007; Sigel and Steinmann, 2012; Sieghart, 2015; Laverty et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature and established scientific knowledge.

claim: Neurosteroids modulate GABAARs by binding to sites within the transmembrane domains.
source: NS modulate GABAARs by binding to sites within the TMDs (Belelli and Lambert, 2005; Mitchell et al., 2008; Akk et al., 2007; Reddy and Estes, 2016; Chen et al., 2019; Miller et al., 2017; Laverty et al., 2017; Hosie et al., 2006; Hosie et al., 2009; Chen et al., 2018; Sugasawa et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature and photolabeling data in the manuscript.

claim: The α subunit transmembrane domains are essential to the actions of PAM-NS.
source: Specifically, the α subunit TMDs are essential to the actions of PAM-NS (Chen et al., 2019; Miller et al., 2017; Laverty et al., 2017; Chen et al., 2018; Sugasawa et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature and mutational data in the manuscript.

claim: Mutagenesis studies in α1β2γ2 GABAARs have identified Q242 and W246 in TM1 of the α1 subunit as critical to neurosteroid potentiation of GABA-elicited currents.
source: Mutagenesis studies in α1β2γ2 GABAARs have identified several residues in the α1 subunit, notably Q242 and W246 in TM1, as critical to NS potentiation of GABA-elicited currents (Hosie et al., 2006; Hosie et al., 2009; Akk et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Crystallographic studies have shown that neurosteroids bind in a cleft between α subunits in homo-pentameric chimeric receptors.
source: Crystallographic studies have subsequently shown that, in homo-pentameric chimeric receptors in which the TMDs are derived from either α1 (Laverty et al., 2017; Chen et al., 2018) or α5 subunits (Miller et al., 2017), the NS 3α,21dihydroxy-5α-pregnan-20-one (3α5α-THDOC), pregnanolone and alphaxalone bind in a cleft between the α subunits, with the C3-hydroxyl substituent of the steroids interacting directly with Q242 in the α subunit (αQ242).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior crystallographic studies.

claim: The C3-hydroxyl substituent of neurosteroids interacts directly with Q242 in the α subunit.
source: Crystallographic studies have subsequently shown that, in homo-pentameric chimeric receptors in which the TMDs are derived from either α1 (Laverty et al., 2017; Chen et al., 2018) or α5 subunits (Miller et al., 2017), the NS 3α,21dihydroxy-5α-pregnan-20-one (3α5α-THDOC), pregnanolone and alphaxalone bind in a cleft between the α subunits, with the C3-hydroxyl substituent of the steroids interacting directly with Q242 in the α subunit (αQ242).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior crystallographic studies.

claim: PAM-NS activate homo-pentameric chimeric receptors, and their action is blocked by αQ242L and αQ242W mutations.
source: PAM-NS activate these chimeric receptors, and their action is blocked by αQ242L and αQ242W mutations.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature and mutational data in the manuscript.

claim: A single canonical intersubunit binding site for neurosteroid action is conserved across the six α subunit isoforms.
source: These studies posit a single canonical intersubunit binding site for NS action that is conserved across the six α subunit isoforms (Miller et al., 2017; Laverty et al., 2017; Chen et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a claim from prior literature that is being contrasted with the current study's findings.

claim: Site-directed mutagenesis has identified multiple disparate residues on GABAARs that affect neurosteroid-induced activation, suggestive of two neurosteroid-binding sites.
source: Site-directed mutagenesis has identified multiple disparate residues on GABAARs that affect NS-induced activation, suggestive of two NS-binding sites: one site mediating potentiation of GABA responses and the other mediating direct activation (Hosie et al., 2006; Hosie et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Single channel electrophysiological studies have identified multiple distinct effects of neurosteroids consistent with multiple neurosteroid-binding sites.
source: Single channel electrophysiological studies (Akk et al., 2007; Akk et al., 2010; Akk et al., 2004) as well as studies examining neurosteroid modulation of [35S]t-butylbicyclophosphorothionate (TBPS) binding (Evers et al., 2010), have also identified multiple distinct effects of NS, with various structural analogues producing some or all of these effects, consistent with multiple NS-binding sites (Hosie et al., 2006; Hosie et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: There are multiple PAM-NS-binding sites on α1β3 GABAARs including an intersubunit site and intrasubunit sites in both α1 and β3 subunits.
source: Our recent photolabeling studies have confirmed that there are multiple PAM-NS-binding sites on α1β3 GABAARs (Chen et al., 2019). In addition to the canonical site at the interface between the TMDs of adjacent subunits (intersubunit site) (Chen et al., 2019; Miller et al., 2017; Laverty et al., 2017; Chen et al., 2018), we identified NS-binding sites within the α-helical bundles of both the α1 and β3 subunits (intrasubunit sites) of α1β3 GABAARs (Chen et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior photolabeling studies by the authors.

claim: 3α5αP binds to all three neurosteroid-binding sites (intersubunit and both intrasubunit sites) on α1β3 GABAARs.
source: 3α5αP binds to all three sites (Chen et al., 2019); mutagenesis of these sites suggests that the intersubunit and α1 intrasubunit sites, but not the β3 intrasubunit site, contribute to 3α5αP PAM activity (Chen et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior photolabeling studies and mutational data in the manuscript.

claim: The intersubunit and α1 intrasubunit sites, but not the β3 intrasubunit site, contribute to 3α5αP PAM activity.
source: 3α5αP binds to all three sites (Chen et al., 2019); mutagenesis of these sites suggests that the intersubunit and α1 intrasubunit sites, but not the β3 intrasubunit site, contribute to 3α5αP PAM activity (Chen et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior mutational studies and data in the manuscript (Figure 6B).

claim: The 3α-hydroxyl group is critical to neurosteroid activation of GABAARs.
source: The 3α-hydroxyl (3α-OH) group is critical to NS activation of GABAARs and 3β-OH NS lack PAM activity (Akk et al., 2007; Wang et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature and data showing 3β5αP, KK148, and KK150 do not potentiate currents (Figure 1B-D).

claim: 3β-OH neurosteroids lack PAM activity.
source: The 3α-hydroxyl (3α-OH) group is critical to NS activation of GABAARs and 3β-OH NS lack PAM activity (Akk et al., 2007; Wang et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature and data showing 3β5αP does not potentiate currents (Figure 1B).

claim: Many 3β-OH neurosteroids are GABAAR NAMs.
source: Indeed, many 3β-OH NS are GABAAR NAMs (Wang et al., 2002; Lundgren et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature and data showing 3β5αP reduces steady-state currents (Figure 2C).

claim: 3β-OH neurosteroids are non-competitive inhibitors with respect to GABA and 3α-OH neurosteroids.
source: While molecular docking studies have suggested that the 3β-OH NS epi-pregnanolone (3β5βP) should compete for binding with PAM-NS (Miller et al., 2017), 3β-OH NS are non-competitive inhibitors with respect to GABA and 3α-OH NS, indicating that they are unlikely to act at the canonical PAM-binding site (Akk et al., 2007; Wang et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Steroids with a sulfate at the 3-carbon are GABAAR NAMs thought to act at sites distinct from GABAAR PAMs.
source: Steroids with a sulfate rather than a hydroxyl at the 3-carbon are also GABAAR NAMs thought to act at sites distinct from GABAAR PAMs (Akk et al., 2007; Akk et al., 2001; Wang et al., 2002; Seljeset et al., 2018; Park-Chung et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Crystallographic studies have demonstrated a possible binding site for pregnenolone sulfate between TM3 and TM4 on the intracellular end of the α-subunit TMD.
source: The precise location of this site is unclear, but crystallographic studies have demonstrated a possible binding site between TM3 and TM4 on the intracellular end of the α-subunit TMD (Seljeset et al., 2018; Laverty et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior crystallographic studies.

claim: 3β-OH neurosteroids and pregnenolone sulfate likely act via interactions with distinct sites.
source: While 3β-OH NS and PS both inhibit GABAARs, they likely act via interactions with distinct sites (Akk et al., 2007; Akk et al., 2001; Wang et al., 2002; Lundgren et al., 2003; Seljeset et al., 2018; Miller et al., 2017; Laverty et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: None of the neurosteroid analogues lacking a 3α-OH potentiated GABA-elicited currents.
source: None of the NS analogues lacking a 3α-OH potentiated GABA-elicited currents (Figure 1B–D).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 1B-D.

claim: Both 3β5αP and KK148 significantly enhanced [3H]muscimol binding.
source: However, both 3β5αP and KK148 significantly enhanced [3H]muscimol binding (Figure 1E).
evidence: Supported by radioligand binding data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: KK150 did not potentiate GABA-elicited currents and minimally enhanced [3H]muscimol binding.
source: KK150, in contrast, did not potentiate GABA-elicited currents and minimally enhanced [3H]muscimol binding (Figure 1D–E).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological and radioligand binding data shown in Figure 1D-E.

claim: Neurosteroid analogues with different stereochemistry or substituents at the 3- and 17-positions show distinct patterns in modulation of α1β3 GABAAR currents and orthosteric ligand binding.
source: Collectively, these data show that, NS analogues with different stereochemistry or substituents at the 3- and 17-positions show distinct patterns in modulation of α1β3 GABAAR currents and orthosteric ligand binding.
evidence: Supported by the combined electrophysiological and binding data for different neurosteroid analogues (Figure 1).

claim: The 3-OH is an important determinant of binding affinity to the site(s) mediating neurosteroid enhancement of [3H]muscimol binding.
source: Notably, the compounds with a 3-OH (3α5αP, 3β5αP) are 10-fold more potent than those with a 3-diazirine (KK148, KK150) in enhancing [3H]muscimol binding (Figure 1E), suggesting that the 3-OH is an important determinant of binding affinity to the site(s) mediating these effects.
evidence: Supported by comparison of EC50 values for different neurosteroids in [3H]muscimol binding assays (Figure 1E, Table 1).

claim: KK148 enhanced [3H]muscimol binding in intact cells as much or more than in permeabilized cells.
source: KK148 enhanced [3H]muscimol binding in intact cells as much or more than in permeabilized cells, indicating that this effect is not a result of selective NS actions on intracellular receptors (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by radioligand binding data comparing intact and permeabilized cells shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: KK148 and 3β5αP both decreased steady-state currents when co-applied with saturating GABA.
source: KK148 and 3β5αP both decreased steady-state currents (Figure 2A and C), whereas KK150 did not (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 2A and 2C.

claim: KK150 did not decrease steady-state currents when co-applied with saturating GABA.
source: KK148 and 3β5αP both decreased steady-state currents (Figure 2A and C), whereas KK150 did not (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Co-application of 3β5αP with 1 mM GABA preferentially inhibited steady-state rather than peak currents.
source: Co-application of 3β5αP with 1 mM GABA preferentially inhibited steady-state rather than peak currents (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The inhibitory effect of 3β5αP was not observed in receptors with the α1(V256S) TM2 pore-lining mutation.
source: The inhibitory effect of 3β5αP was not observed in receptors with the α1(V256S) TM2 pore-lining mutation, which was previously shown to remove the inhibitory effects of sulfated steroids (Akk et al., 2001; Wang et al., 2002; Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 2D and citations to prior literature.

claim: The α1(V256S)β3 mutation eliminated [3H]muscimol binding enhancement by 3β5αP but not 3α5αP.
source: Consistent with this, the α1(V256S)β3 mutation which abolishes NS-induced inhibition (Akk et al., 2001; Wang et al., 2002) eliminated [3H]muscimol binding enhancement by 3β5αP but not 3α5αP (Figure 3).
evidence: Supported by radioligand binding data shown in Figure 3 and citations to prior literature.

claim: 3α5αP increases [3H]muscimol binding by stabilizing an active state of the receptor.
source: We infer that 3α5αP increases [3H]muscimol binding by stabilizing an active state of the receptor.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that 3α5αP enhances binding and this effect is not eliminated by the α1(V256S) mutation that prevents desensitization.

claim: 3β5αP increases [3H]muscimol binding by stabilizing a desensitized state of the receptor.
source: In contrast, 3β5αP increases [3H]muscimol binding by stabilizing a desensitized state of the receptor; this effect is eliminated in the α1(V256S)β3 receptor.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that 3β5αP enhances binding and this effect is eliminated by the α1(V256S) mutation that prevents desensitization.

claim: 3β5αP and KK148 enhance orthosteric ligand affinity by stabilizing a desensitized state of the GABAAR.
source: These data indicate that 3β5αP and KK148 enhance orthosteric ligand affinity by stabilizing a desensitized state of the GABAAR.
evidence: Supported by combined electrophysiological and binding data showing these compounds enhance [3H]muscimol binding and reduce steady-state currents.

claim: Enhancement of [3H]muscimol binding by 10 μM 3β5αP is slow, with a time constant of approximately 4 minutes at 4°C.
source: Enhancement of [3H]muscimol binding by 10 µM 3β5αP is slow, with a time constant of 4 min at 4°C (τ = 3.97 ± 0.15 min: mean ± SEM, n = 4, Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by time course experiments shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Application of 1 mM GABA elicited a current response with a peak Popen of 0.71 ± 0.25 in α1β3 GABAARs.
source: Application of 1 mM GABA elicited a current response that had a peak Popen of 0.71 ± 0.25 (mean ± SD; n = 16).
evidence: Calculated from electrophysiological recordings.

claim: The steady-state Popen with 1 mM GABA was 0.121 ± 0.033 in α1β3 GABAARs.
source: The Popen of the steady-state response was 0.121 ± 0.033 (n = 7), that was reduced to 0.077 ± 0.013 (n = 5) with 3 µM 3β5αP.
evidence: Calculated from electrophysiological recordings.

claim: 3 µM 3β5αP reduced steady-state Popen to 0.077 ± 0.013 in α1β3 GABAARs activated by 1 mM GABA.
source: The Popen of the steady-state response was 0.121 ± 0.033 (n = 7), that was reduced to 0.077 ± 0.013 (n = 5) with 3 µM 3β5αP.
evidence: Calculated from electrophysiological recordings.

claim: The steady-state Pdesensitized is 0.829 in the presence of 1 mM GABA and 0.892 in the presence of GABA + 3β5αP.
source: Analysis of steady-state currents using the Resting-Open-Desensitized model indicates that the steady-state Pdesensitized is 0.829 in the presence of GABA, and 0.892 in the presence of GABA + steroid.
evidence: Calculated from electrophysiological data using a kinetic model.

claim: Application of 20 nM muscimol elicited a peak response with Popen of 0.012 ± 0.004 in α1β3 GABAARs.
source: The application of 20 nM muscimol elicited a peak response with Popen of 0.012 ± 0.004 (n = 6).
evidence: Calculated from electrophysiological recordings.

claim: 3 µM 3β5αP reduced the steady-state Popen from 0.011 ± 0.004 to 0.009 ± 0.004 in α1β3 GABAARs activated by 20 nM muscimol.
source: The steady-state Popen was 0.011 ± 0.004. In the same cells, subsequent exposure to 3 µM 3β5αP reduced the steady-state Popen to 0.009 ± 0.004 (p=0.0174; paired t-test).
evidence: Calculated from electrophysiological recordings.

claim: The calculated steady-state Pdesensitized was 0.1001 in the presence of 20 nM muscimol and 0.2168 in the presence of muscimol + 3β5αP.
source: The calculated steady-state Pdesensitized was 0.1001 in the presence of muscimol, and 0.2168 in the presence of muscimol + 3β5αP.
evidence: Calculated from electrophysiological data using a kinetic model.

claim: There is a predicted two-fold increase in the sum of (Popen + Pdesensitized) when 3β5αP is combined with 20 nM muscimol.
source: Thus, there is a predicted two-fold increase in the sum of (Popen + Pdesensitized) when the steroid is combined with muscimol, consistent with the doubling of muscimol binding caused by 3β5αP in the [3H]muscimol binding experiments (Figure 1E).
evidence: Calculated from electrophysiological data and compared to binding data.

claim: KK148, KK150, 3α5αP and 3β5αP all prevented KK200 photolabeling of α1N408 in the α1 intrasubunit site.
source: KK148, KK150, 3α5αP and 3β5αP all prevented KK200 photolabeling of α1N408 in the α1 intrasubunit site (Figure 4B), consistent with their binding to this site.
evidence: Supported by photolabeling competition experiments shown in Figure 4B.

claim: KK148, KK150 and 3α5αP but not 3β5αP prevented labeling of β3G308 in the intersubunit site.
source: In contrast, KK148, KK150 and 3α5αP but not 3β5αP prevented labeling of β3G308 in the intersubunit site (Figure 4C), indicating that 3β5αP does not bind to the intersubunit site.
evidence: Supported by photolabeling competition experiments shown in Figure 4C.

claim: KK148 and KK150 photolabeled Y415 in the α1 intrasubunit site.
source: Product ion (MS2) spectra of the KK148- and KK150-labeled peptides from the α1 subunit identified the labeled residue as Y415 for both KK148 and KK150 with photolabeling efficiencies of 0.77% and 0.62%, respectively (Figure 4D–E, Figure 4—figure supplement 2); Y415 is the same residue labeled by KK123 at the α1 intrasubunit site (Chen et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by mass spectrometry analysis of photolabeled peptides shown in Figure 4D-E.

claim: KK148 and KK150 photolabeled the β3 intrasubunit site.
source: The KK148 and KK150 labeled peptides in TM4 of the β3 subunit and corresponding unlabeled peptide were identified by fragmentation spectra as β3TM4 I426-N445. These data support labeling of the β3 intrasubunit site by KK148 and KK150.
evidence: Supported by mass spectrometry analysis of photolabeled peptides shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: 3β5αP completely inhibited KK123 photolabeling at both α1 and β3 intrasubunit sites.
source: 3β5αP completely inhibited KK123 photolabeling at both intrasubunit sites (Figure 5B–C).
evidence: Supported by photolabeling competition experiments shown in Figure 5B-C.

claim: KK148, KK150 and 3α5αP bind to all three of the identified neurosteroid-binding sites.
source: Collectively, the data show that KK148, KK150 and 3α5αP bind to all three of the identified NS-binding sites.
evidence: Supported by photolabeling competition experiments (Figures 4 and 5).

claim: 3β5αP selectively binds to the two intrasubunit binding sites, but not to the canonical β3(+)–α1(-) intersubunit site.
source: In contrast, 3β5αP selectively binds to the two intrasubunit binding sites, but not to the canonical β3(+)–α1(-) intersubunit site.
evidence: Supported by photolabeling competition experiments (Figures 4 and 5).

claim: None of the mutations targeting neurosteroid-binding sites produced a significant change in [3H]muscimol Kd.
source: None of these mutations produced a significant change in [3H]muscimol Kd (Figure 7B and Figure 7—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by radioligand binding isotherms shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Mutations in the β3(+)–α1(-) intersubunit and α1 intrasubunit sites decreased 3α5αP enhancement of [3H]muscimol binding by approximately 80%.
source: Mutations in the β3(+)–α1(-) intersubunit and α1 intrasubunit sites decreased 3α5αP enhancement of [3H]muscimol binding by ~80%, while mutation of the β3 intrasubunit site led to a small decrease (Figure 6B, Table 1).
evidence: Supported by radioligand binding data shown in Figure 6B and Table 1.

claim: Mutation of the β3 intrasubunit site led to a small decrease in 3α5αP enhancement of [3H]muscimol binding.
source: Mutations in the β3(+)–α1(-) intersubunit and α1 intrasubunit sites decreased 3α5αP enhancement of [3H]muscimol binding by ~80%, while mutation of the β3 intrasubunit site led to a small decrease (Figure 6B, Table 1).
evidence: Supported by radioligand binding data shown in Figure 6B and Table 1.

claim: Mutations in the α1 and β3 intrasubunit sites, but not the intersubunit site, decreased the enhancement of [3H]muscimol binding by 3β5αP and KK148.
source: In contrast, mutations in the α1 and β3 intrasubunit sites, but not the intersubunit site decreased the enhancement of [3H]muscimol binding by 3β5αP and KK148 (Figure 6C–D, Table 1).
evidence: Supported by radioligand binding data shown in Figure 6C-D and Table 1.

claim: The α1β3(M286W) mutation abolished [3H]muscimol binding enhancement by etomidate.
source: The mutations targeting NS-binding sites resulted in modest decreases in [3H]muscimol binding enhancement by etomidate; however, the α1β3(M286W) mutation which abolishes etomidate potentiation and activation of GABAARs (Stewart et al., 2008; Ziemba et al., 2018), also abolished [3H]muscimol binding enhancement (Figure 6E).
evidence: Supported by radioligand binding data shown in Figure 6E and citations to prior literature.

claim: KK150 inhibited enhancement of [3H]muscimol binding by 3α5αP and KK148.
source: Consistent with this prediction, KK150 inhibited enhancement of [3H]muscimol binding by 3α5αP and KK148 (Figure 8).
evidence: Supported by radioligand binding competition experiments shown in Figure 8.

claim: Multiple neurosteroid-binding sites contribute to enhancement of [3H]muscimol affinity.
source: Collectively, these results show that multiple NS-binding sites contribute to enhancement of [3H]muscimol affinity and that potentiating NS (3α5αP) and non-potentiating NS (3β5αP, KK148 and KK150) have both common and distinct sites of action.
evidence: Supported by mutational analysis of different neurosteroid-binding sites (Figure 6, Table 1).

claim: 3α5αP enhances [3H]muscimol binding through all three sites but predominantly through the intersubunit and α1 intrasubunit sites.
source: Specifically, 3α5αP enhances [3H]muscimol binding through all three sites but predominantly through the intersubunit and α1 intrasubunit sites, which we have previously shown mediate PAM-NS potentiation (Chen et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by mutational analysis shown in Figure 6B and Table 1.

claim: 3β5αP and KK148 enhance [3H]muscimol binding exclusively through the α1 and β3 intrasubunit sites.
source: In contrast, 3β5αP and KK148 enhance [3H]muscimol binding exclusively through the α1 and β3 intrasubunit sites.
evidence: Supported by mutational analysis shown in Figure 6C-D and Table 1.

claim: KK150 antagonizes the effects of KK148 on [3H]muscimol binding, presumably via the intrasubunit sites.
source: KK150 antagonizes the effects of KK148 on [3H]muscimol binding, presumably via the intrasubunit sites, and antagonizes the effects of 3α5αP, possibly via all three sites.
evidence: Supported by competition binding experiments shown in Figure 8.

claim: KK150 antagonizes the effects of 3α5αP on [3H]muscimol binding, possibly via all three sites.
source: KK150 antagonizes the effects of KK148 on [3H]muscimol binding, presumably via the intrasubunit sites, and antagonizes the effects of 3α5αP, possibly via all three sites.
evidence: Supported by competition binding experiments shown in Figure 8.

claim: Membranes containing WT receptors have 10–20-fold higher [3H]muscimol binding (Bmax) than membranes containing α1(N408A/Y411F)β3 receptors.
source: The raw data show that membranes containing WT receptors have 10–20-fold higher [3H]muscimol binding (Bmax) than membranes containing α1(N408A/Y411F)β3 receptors (Figure 7A), whereas the Bmax of membranes containing α1(Q242L)β3, α1β3(Y284F) or α1(V227W)β3 receptors was the same as for WT α1β3 GABAARs (Figure 7—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by radioligand binding isotherms shown in Figure 7A.

claim: The α1(N408A/Y411F)β3 mutations did not have a significant effect on [3H]muscimol affinity.
source: The α1(N408A/Y411F)β3 mutations did not have a significant effect on [3H]muscimol affinity (Figure 7B), but eliminated the modulatory effects of NS (3α5αP and KK148) on [3H]muscimol affinity (Figure 7C–D and Figure 7—source data 2).
evidence: Supported by normalized radioligand binding isotherms shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The α1(N408A/Y411F)β3 mutations eliminated the modulatory effects of neurosteroids (3α5αP and KK148) on [3H]muscimol affinity.
source: The α1(N408A/Y411F)β3 mutations did not have a significant effect on [3H]muscimol affinity (Figure 7B), but eliminated the modulatory effects of NS (3α5αP and KK148) on [3H]muscimol affinity (Figure 7C–D and Figure 7—source data 2).
evidence: Supported by radioligand binding isotherms with and without neurosteroids shown in Figure 7C-D.

claim: Etomidate enhanced [3H]muscimol affinity in both the WT and α1(N408A/Y411F)β3 receptors.
source: Etomidate enhanced [3H]muscimol affinity in both the WT and α1(N408A/Y411F)β3 receptors, indicating that the effect of these mutations are specific to NS action (Figure 7C–D).
evidence: Supported by radioligand binding isotherms with etomidate shown in Figure 7C-D.

claim: 3β5αP produced a small reduction in steady-state current in α1(Q242L)β3 receptors.
source: 3α5αP produced a small reduction in steady-state current in α1(Q242L)β3 receptors with mutations in neither of the intrasubunit sites (Figure 10A).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 10A.

claim: The inhibitory effect of 3α5αP in α1(Q242L)β3 receptors was eliminated by α1(V256S)β3.
source: This inhibitory effect was eliminated by α1(V256S)β3, indicating that it was due to receptor desensitization (Figure 10D).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 10D.

claim: In receptors with combined mutations in the intersubunit and α1 intrasubunit sites, 3α5αP significantly inhibited the steady-state current.
source: In receptors with combined mutations in the intersubunit and α1 intrasubunit sites [i.e. α1(Q242L/N408A/Y411F)β3], 3α5αP significantly inhibited the steady-state current (Figure 10B), an effect that was markedly reduced by mutations in the β3 intrasubunit site [α1(Q242L)β3(Y284F)] (Figure 10C).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 10B.

claim: The inhibitory effect of 3α5αP in α1(Q242L/N408A/Y411F)β3 receptors was markedly reduced by mutations in the β3 intrasubunit site.
source: In receptors with combined mutations in the intersubunit and α1 intrasubunit sites [i.e. α1(Q242L/N408A/Y411F)β3], 3α5αP significantly inhibited the steady-state current (Figure 10B), an effect that was markedly reduced by mutations in the β3 intrasubunit site [α1(Q242L)β3(Y284F)] (Figure 10C).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 10C.

claim: 3α5αP exerts a desensitizing effect by binding to the β3 intrasubunit site.
source: These data suggest that 3α5αP exerts a desensitizing effect by binding to the β3 intrasubunit site and that 3α5αP binding to the α1 intrasubunit site does not promote desensitization (Figure 10D).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological recordings with various mutations shown in Figure 10.

claim: 3α5αP binding to the α1 intrasubunit site does not promote desensitization.
source: These data suggest that 3α5αP exerts a desensitizing effect by binding to the β3 intrasubunit site and that 3α5αP binding to the α1 intrasubunit site does not promote desensitization (Figure 10D).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological recordings with various mutations shown in Figure 10.

claim: Enhanced desensitization by the PAM-NS 3α5αP has been observed in prior studies.
source: Enhanced desensitization by the PAM-NS 3α5αP (Haage and Johansson, 1999) and 3α5α-THDOC (Zhu and Vicini, 1997; Bianchi and Macdonald, 2003) has been observed in prior studies supporting the current finding with 3α5αP.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The selective binding of 3β5αP to a subset of identified neurosteroid-binding sites provides an explanation for its NAM activity.
source: The selective binding of 3β5αP to a subset of identified NS-binding sites provides an explanation for its NAM activity.
evidence: Inferred from the combined photolabeling and functional data showing 3β5αP binds only to intrasubunit sites and promotes desensitization.

claim: 3β5αP stabilizes desensitized receptors by binding to the α1 and β3 intrasubunit sites.
source: 3β5αP stabilizes desensitized receptors by binding to the α1 and β3 intrasubunit sites, but does not activate the receptor because it does not bind to the intersubunit site.
evidence: Supported by photolabeling data showing 3β5αP binds to intrasubunit sites (Figures 4-5) and functional data showing it promotes desensitization (Figure 9).

claim: 3β5αP does not activate the receptor because it does not bind to the intersubunit site.
source: 3β5αP stabilizes desensitized receptors by binding to the α1 and β3 intrasubunit sites, but does not activate the receptor because it does not bind to the intersubunit site.
evidence: Supported by photolabeling data showing 3β5αP does not bind to the intersubunit site (Figure 4C) and functional data showing it does not potentiate currents (Figure 1B).

claim: Docking and free energy perturbation calculations predicted that 3β5βP binds to the intersubunit site with free energies equivalent to pregnanolone.
source: First, docking and free energy perturbation calculations in a prior study predicted that 3β5βP binds to the intersubunit site in a similar orientation and with free energies of binding that are equivalent to pregnanolone (3α5βP) (Miller et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior computational study.

claim: Docking studies show similar binding energies and orientations of 3β5αP and 3α5αP binding in the β3(+)–α1(-) intersubunit site.
source: Our docking studies also show similar binding energies and orientations of 3β5αP and 3α5αP binding in the β3(+)–α1(-) intersubunit site of either a homology model of the α1β3 receptor or the cryo-EM structure (PDB ID: 6I53) of the α1β3γ2 receptor in a lipid nanodisc (Laverty et al., 2019; Figure 11).
evidence: Supported by computational docking studies shown in Figure 11.

claim: Binding affinity or docking scores of neurosteroids binding to the intersubunit site are not significantly affected by mutations that eliminate neurosteroid activation.
source: We have also shown that binding affinity or docking scores of NS binding to the intersubunit site are not significantly affected by mutations (α1Q242L, α1Q242W, α1W246L) that eliminate NS activation, although binding orientation is altered (Sugasawa et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior study by the authors.

claim: Neurosteroid binding in the intersubunit site is tolerant to significant changes in critical residues and neurosteroid ligand structure.
source: These data indicate that NS binding in the intersubunit site is tolerant to significant changes in critical residues and NS ligand structure, and are consistent with our findings that NS analogues, such as KK148 and KK150, can bind to the intersubunit site but have no effect on activation (Figures 1 and 4).
evidence: Inferred from combined computational and experimental data.

claim: Lipid binding to intrasubunit pockets in bacterial pLGICs modulates receptor desensitization.
source: Interestingly, lipid binding to intrasubunit pockets in bacterial pLGICs analogous to the α1 and β3 intrasubunit sites in GABAAR, also modulates receptor desensitization; docosahexaenoic acid binding to an intrasubunit site in GLIC (Basak et al., 2017) and phosphatidylglycerol in ELIC (Tong et al., 2019) increase and decrease agonist-induced desensitization, respectively.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior studies on bacterial pLGICs.

claim: The effects of various neurosteroid analogues are a consequence of their efficacy at each of the sites they occupy.
source: The combined results of mutational analyses and binding data demonstrate that the effects of various NS analogues are also a consequence of their efficacy at each of the sites they occupy.
evidence: Inferred from the combined mutational, binding, and functional data.

claim: KK148 should act as a competitive antagonist to PAM-NS at the intersubunit site.
source: This model predicts that KK148 should act as a competitive antagonist to PAM-NS at the intersubunit site.
evidence: Predicted from the model showing KK148 binds to the intersubunit site without efficacy.

claim: KK150 should be a competitive neurosteroid antagonist at all three binding sites.
source: This model also predicts that KK150 should be a competitive NS antagonist at all three binding sites. Consistent with this prediction, KK150 antagonizes 3α5αP and KK148 enhancement of [3H]muscimol binding (Figure 8).
evidence: Predicted from the model and supported by competition binding data shown in Figure 8.

claim: At a synapse, GABAARs are transiently exposed to high (mM) concentrations of GABA leading to a channel Popen approaching one.
source: At a synapse, GABAARs are transiently exposed to high (mM) concentrations of GABA leading to a channel Popen approaching one (Farrant and Nusser, 2005; Feng and Forman, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature and established scientific knowledge.

claim: GABA is quickly cleared from the synapse leading to rapid deactivation with minimal desensitization.
source: GABA is quickly cleared from the synapse leading to rapid deactivation with minimal desensitization (Jones and Westbrook, 1995; Overstreet et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature and established scientific knowledge.

claim: In the presence of a PAM-NS, deactivation is slowed, resulting in a prolongation of the IPSC and increased inhibitory current.
source: In the presence of a PAM-NS, deactivation is slowed, resulting in a prolongation of the IPSC and increased inhibitory current (Harrison et al., 1987a; Zhu and Vicini, 1997; Harrison et al., 1987b; Chakrabarti et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: PAM-NS prolong the slow component of GABAAR desensitization and slow recovery from desensitization.
source: A second effect has been observed in which the PAM-NS 3α5αP (Haage and Johansson, 1999) and 3α5α-THDOC (Zhu and Vicini, 1997) prolong the slow component of GABAAR desensitization and slow recovery from desensitization.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: PAM-NS increase late channel openings and IPSC prolongation.
source: This results in increased late channel openings (Zhu and Vicini, 1997; Jones and Westbrook, 1995) and IPSC prolongation (Harrison et al., 1987b; Chakrabarti et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: When the frequency of synaptic firing is rapid, the desensitizing effect of neurosteroids may contribute to frequency-dependent reduction in IPSC amplitude.
source: When the frequency of synaptic firing is rapid, the desensitizing effect of NS may also contribute to frequency-dependent reduction in IPSC amplitude (Zhu and Vicini, 1997; Jones and Westbrook, 1996).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Computational docking of 3α5αP indicates a rank order affinity of: intersubunit > α1 intrasubunit > β3 intrasubunit sites.
source: Computational docking of 3α5αP to these sites indicates modest differences in affinity between the sites with a rank order affinity of: intersubunit > α1 intrasubunit > β3 intrasubunit sites (Figure 11—source data 1; Chen et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by computational docking studies and citation to prior work.

claim: Mutational analysis indicates that 3α5αP has a lower affinity to the β3 intrasubunit site.
source: Mutational analysis of the effects of NS on enhancement of [3H]muscimol binding also indicates that 3α5αP has a lower affinity to the β3 intrasubunit site (Figure 6B, Table 1).
evidence: Inferred from the observation that mutations in the β3 intrasubunit site have a smaller effect on 3α5αP enhancement of binding compared to other sites.

claim: Binding to the β3 intrasubunit site may serve as a negative feedback mechanism preventing excessive PAM-NS effects on synaptic currents.
source: Thus ,binding to the β3 intrasubunit site may serve as a negative feedback mechanism preventing excessive PAM-NS effects on synaptic currents.
evidence: Speculated based on the observation that 3α5αP binding to the β3 intrasubunit site promotes desensitization.

claim: There are no available structures of a heteropentameric GABAAR with a bound neurosteroid.
source: While several high-resolution structures of αβγ GABAARs in a lipidic environment (nano-discs) with bound orthosteric or allosteric ligands have been published (Laverty et al., 2019; Masiulis et al., 2019; Kim et al., 2020), there are no available structures of a heteropentameric GABAAR with a bound NS.
evidence: Supported by citations to available structural studies and the absence of heteropentameric structures with neurosteroids.

claim: Three X-ray structures of homopentameric, chimeric GABAARs show neurosteroids bound only in the intersubunit site.
source: There are, however, three X-ray structures of homopentameric, chimeric GABAARs crystallized from detergent, all showing NS bound only in the intersubunit site (Miller et al., 2017; Laverty et al., 2017; Chen et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior crystallographic studies.

claim: An α1 intrasubunit neurosteroid binding site has been identified in a detergent-solubilized ELIC-α1 chimeric receptor.
source: However, we have also identified an α1 intrasubunit NS binding site using a 3α5αP analogue photolabeling reagent in a detergent-solubilized ELIC-α1 chimeric receptor (Sugasawa et al., 2019), indicating that NS can bind to this site in a detergent-solubilized chimeric receptor.
evidence: Supported by citation to prior photolabeling study by the authors.

claim: The actions of inhibitory and potentiating neurosteroids in αβγ or αβδ receptors are qualitatively similar to those observed in αβ receptors.
source: It is also important to consider that our analyses of the functional effects of NS binding were performed using α1β3 GABAARs. While the actions of inhibitory and potentiating NS in αβγ or αβδ receptors are qualitatively similar to those observed in αβ receptors, the trimeric receptors may have one less intrasubunit NS-binding site per pentamer, or an intrasubunit with different NS specificity or effect.
evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge and inference from the current study.

claim: Trimeric GABAARs may have one less intrasubunit neurosteroid-binding site per pentamer, or an intrasubunit site with different neurosteroid specificity or effect.
source: While the actions of inhibitory and potentiating NS in αβγ or αβδ receptors are qualitatively similar to those observed in αβ receptors, the trimeric receptors may have one less intrasubunit NS-binding site per pentamer, or an intrasubunit with different NS specificity or effect.
evidence: Speculated based on the structural differences between αβ and αβγ receptors.

claim: The presence of a γ-subunit has been shown to alter the conformational symmetry of the GABAAR.
source: Additionally, the presence of a γ-subunit has been shown to alter the conformational symmetry of the GABAAR (Laverty et al., 2019; Kim et al., 2020; Zhu et al., 2018) and may influence NS binding to an intrasubunit site or its functional effects.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior structural studies.

claim: The presence of a γ-subunit may influence neurosteroid binding to an intrasubunit site or its functional effects.
source: Additionally, the presence of a γ-subunit has been shown to alter the conformational symmetry of the GABAAR (Laverty et al., 2019; Kim et al., 2020; Zhu et al., 2018) and may influence NS binding to an intrasubunit site or its functional effects.
evidence: Speculated based on the known structural effects of the γ-subunit.

claim: Different neurosteroid analogues selectively bind to subsets of three sites on the α1β3 GABAAR, with each analogue exhibiting state-dependent binding at a given site.
source: In summary, this study describes a unique NS pharmacology in which different NS analogues selectively bind to subsets of three sites on the α1β3 GABAAR, with each analogue exhibiting state-dependent binding at a given site.
evidence: Supported by the combined photolabeling, binding, and functional data throughout the manuscript.

claim: The combination of site-selectivity and state-dependence of binding determines whether a neurosteroid analogue is a PAM, a NAM or an antagonist of neurosteroid action at the GABAAR.
source: The combination of site-selectivity and state-dependence of binding determines whether a NS analogue is a PAM, a NAM or an antagonist of NS action at the GABAAR.
evidence: Supported by the combined data showing different functional outcomes for different neurosteroids based on their binding patterns.

claim: Other GABAAR subunit isoforms and heteropentameric subunit combinations will likely reveal additional neurosteroid-binding sites with distinct affinity and state-dependence for various analogues.
source: It seems likely that other GABAAR subunit isoforms and heteropentameric subunit combinations will reveal additional NS-binding sites with distinct affinity and state-dependence for various analogues.
evidence: Speculated based on the findings in α1β3 receptors and known diversity of GABAAR subtypes.

claim: The identification of potent agonists and antagonists for each neurosteroid-binding site will provide tools for understanding the biological effects of endogenous neurosteroids.
source: The identification of potent agonists and antagonists for each of these sites will provide tools for understanding the biological effects of endogenous neurosteroids and potentially for the development of precision neurosteroid therapeutics.
evidence: Speculated based on the implications of the current findings.

claim: The identification of potent agonists and antagonists for each neurosteroid-binding site has potential for the development of precision neurosteroid therapeutics.
source: The identification of potent agonists and antagonists for each of these sites will provide tools for understanding the biological effects of endogenous neurosteroids and potentially for the development of precision neurosteroid therapeutics.
evidence: Speculated based on the implications of the current findings.

claim: Mutations in the α1 and β3 intrasubunit sites prevented 3β5αP-enhanced desensitization by approximately 67%.
source: Mutations in the α1 and β3 intrasubunit sites [i.e. α1(N408A/Y411F)β3 and α1β3(Y284F), respectively] prevented 3β5αP-enhanced desensitization by ~67% (Figure 9B), whereas mutation in the β(+)–α(-) intersubunit site [α1(Q242L)β3] was without effect (Figure 9B).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 9B.

claim: Mutation in the β(+)–α(-) intersubunit site was without effect on 3β5αP-enhanced desensitization.
source: Mutations in the α1 and β3 intrasubunit sites [i.e. α1(N408A/Y411F)β3 and α1β3(Y284F), respectively] prevented 3β5αP-enhanced desensitization by ~67% (Figure 9B), whereas mutation in the β(+)–α(-) intersubunit site [α1(Q242L)β3] was without effect (Figure 9B).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 9B.

claim: Receptors with mutations in both the α1 and β3 intrasubunit sites showed less neurosteroid-enhancement of desensitization than receptors with mutations in either of the intrasubunit sites alone.
source: Receptors with mutations in both the α1 and β3 intrasubunit sites [α1(N408A/Y411F)β3(Y284F)] showed less NS-enhancement of desensitization than receptors with mutations in either of the intrasubunit sites alone, indicating that both intrasubunit sites contribute to the desensitizing effect (Figure 9B).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 9B.

claim: Both α1 and β3 intrasubunit sites contribute to the desensitizing effect of 3β5αP.
source: Receptors with mutations in both the α1 and β3 intrasubunit sites [α1(N408A/Y411F)β3(Y284F)] showed less NS-enhancement of desensitization than receptors with mutations in either of the intrasubunit sites alone, indicating that both intrasubunit sites contribute to the desensitizing effect (Figure 9B).
evidence: Inferred from the additive effect of mutations in both intrasubunit sites.

claim: The desensitizing effect of 3β5αP is completely eliminated by the V2'S mutation α1(V256S)β3.
source: Although the desensitizing effect of 3β5αP is completely eliminated by the V2'S mutation α1(V256S)β3, it is not completely eliminated by combined mutations of all three binding sites [α1(Q242L/N408A/Y411F)β3(Y284F)] (Figure 9B).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 9B.

claim: The desensitizing effect of 3β5αP is not completely eliminated by combined mutations of all three binding sites.
source: Although the desensitizing effect of 3β5αP is completely eliminated by the V2'S mutation α1(V256S)β3, it is not completely eliminated by combined mutations of all three binding sites [α1(Q242L/N408A/Y411F)β3(Y284F)] (Figure 9B).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 9B.

claim: There may be additional unidentified neurosteroid-binding sites contributing to desensitization.
source: This suggests either that the effects of the mutations are incomplete or there are additional unidentified NS-binding sites contributing to desensitization.
evidence: Speculated based on the observation that combined mutations do not completely eliminate the effect.

claim: KK148 increased GABAAR desensitization with a percent desensitization of 27.2 ± 6.0.
source: Furthermore, KK148 increased GABAAR desensitization (% of desensitization = 27.2 ± 6.0: mean ± SEM, n = 3, Figure 2A) and the α1(V256S)β3 mutation abolished the effect (% of desensitization = 0, n = 1).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The α1(V256S)β3 mutation abolished the desensitizing effect of KK148.
source: Furthermore, KK148 increased GABAAR desensitization (% of desensitization = 27.2 ± 6.0: mean ± SEM, n = 3, Figure 2A) and the α1(V256S)β3 mutation abolished the effect (% of desensitization = 0, n = 1).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological data.

claim: KK150 showed a very small effect on desensitization with a percent desensitization of 2.1 ± 0.7.
source: In contrast, KK150 showed a very small effect on desensitization (% of desensitization = 2.1 ± 0.7: mean ± SEM, n = 5, Figure 2B), consistent with the small increase in [3H]muscimol binding by KK150 (Figure 1E).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 2B.
